item.title: When Recovery Becomes the New Normal After Cannabis and Alcohol
item.description:
Alcoholism

When Recovery Becomes the New Normal After Cannabis and Alcohol

All addictions narrow the reward landscape. Recovery expands it again.

Posted July 14, 2026

Key points
  • The same neuroplasticity allowing addiction to develop also enables the brain to recover from cannabis.
  • Recovery means learning a healthier brain state by rebuilding reward, motivation, sleep, and flexibility.
  • GLP-1 drugs may aid recovery but work best alongside lasting behavior change.

In my previous post, I suggested that regular cannabis use gradually shifts the brain into a new adaptive operating state—one in which the brain comes to expect and demand THC as part of everyday function. If that hypothesis is correct, an equally important question follows: What happens when cannabis is removed? How does the brain learn recovery?

One week after stopping daily cannabis use, a recovering physician looked at me with obvious frustration, saying, "I thought I'd feel better by now." He was no longer intoxicated, but he wasn't sleeping well. Food wasn't appealing to him. Sex wasn't enjoyable. His motivation was low, his attention wandered, and very few things in his life seemed rewarding. Even though he was a physician, like many patients, he wondered whether he had permanently damaged his brain.

Many patients feel worse during the first weeks of abstinence than they expected. They often assume that since cannabis has left their body, recovery should be complete, but often they have insomnia, irritability, reduced appetite, poor concentration, and diminished pleasure. These symptoms reflect the mismatch between a brain that has adapted to THC and a brain that is now learning to function without it.

He needed to understand this key point: Recovery takes time. Most likely, his brain was doing what healthy brains have always done—adapting to life without cannabis. Recovery is building a healthier, adaptive brain state.

In my previous post, I discussed new research suggesting daily cannabis use may gradually shift the brain into an adapted operating state. If that idea is correct, then recovery is not simply the disappearance of intoxication. Recovery itself is another form of neuroplasticity. The brain must learn to function without the drug it had come to demand and expect.

The Adaptive Brain-State Model of Cannabis Addiction and Recovery
Source: Mark Gold, MD with permission

Recovery Is Not the Reverse of Intoxication

One of the most common misconceptions about addiction is that once a drug leaves the body, the brain immediately returns to normal. And that is rarely how recovery works. Repeated exposure to THC produces adaptive changes throughout the endocannabinoid system, including lowered availability of CB1 receptors. Research suggests these receptors gradually recover during abstinence, but recovery takes weeks, not days. Brain imaging studies also indicate repeated cannabis exposure alters communication among the networks involved in attention, executive control, and self-monitoring. If cannabis use stops, these networks gradually regain flexibility.

Clinical recovery follows a similar pattern. Withdrawal symptoms often improve within days, and receptor recovery continues over weeks, while restoring sleep, attention, motivation, and the ability to experience natural rewards may take considerably longer—especially after years of heavy use or regular cannabis use beginning during adolescence. Persistent symptoms should not be mistaken for permanent injury. Instead, they commonly reflect a brain that’s relearning life sober.

The Brain Learns What It Repeats

One principle explains both addiction and recovery: the brain learns what it repeats.

Practice strengthens neural circuits. Musicians refine motor networks by practicing. Athletes improve through repetitions and drills. Learning a new language changes the brain. So does addiction.

After months or years of repeated cannabis (or other drug use), the brain learns that THC helps regulate sleep, reduce stress, relieve boredom, stimulate appetite or libido, or quiet anxiety. Over time, these responses become increasingly automatic.

Recovery requires learning something different. Sleep must become restorative without THC. Exercise must become rewarding again. Relationships, conversation, work, curiosity, music, and purpose must once again activate the brain's natural reward systems. Recovery is not simply giving something up.

It’s also rebuilding an entire sphere of natural rewards.

Recovery Expands the Reward Landscape

One reason addiction becomes so powerful is that life gradually becomes organized around a single, highly reliable source of reward. As that reward becomes dominant, fewer ordinary experiences successfully compete with it. Recovery gradually reverses this process.

Recovery restores the brain's natural diversity of reward. Instead of relying on a single pharmacologic reinforcer, the recovering brain gradually learns to find value again in relationships, work, exercise, music, food, curiosity, and purpose.

Instead of relying on a single pharmacologic reinforcer like cannabis, the brain gradually becomes responsive again to many smaller, naturally rewarding, and diverse experiences—a walk with a friend, finishing meaningful work, playing with your children, listening to or helping another person.

None of these produces the immediate intensity of a psychoactive drug. Together, however, they create something drugs cannot provide: a rich, flexible, and resilient reward system.

Patients who recover and adapt to life without cannabis rarely describe an epiphany, but instead often recognize recovery in retrospect. One day, they realize they enjoyed dinner, laughed with a friend, or woke up looking forward to work. Those ordinary moments often mark extraordinary changes in the recovering brain.

Can We Help the Brain Recover?

Behavioral treatments remain the foundation of recovery. Cognitive behavioral therapy, motivational enhancement, contingency management, rigorous exercise, improved sleep, recovery communities, and meaningful social connection all provide the repeated experiences through which the brain gradually rewires itself.

Neuroscience is now asking an additional question: How do medications help support this process?

One of the most intriguing developments involves GLP-1 receptor agonists, medications originally developed to treat diabetes and obesity, which are now recognized to have GLP-1 signaling that extends well beyond eating behavior, into brain circuits involved in motivation, reward, and reinforcement. Rather than simply reducing appetite, GLP-1 signaling appears to influence how the brain determines that enough reward has been obtained. They are being tested for cannabis use disorders.

GLP-1 receptor agonists may provide a biological window that makes it easier for patients to practice recovery long enough for neuroplasticity to do its slower work. These medications are unlikely to replace behavioral treatments, but they may eventually become valuable partners in recovery.

The same adaptive principles may ultimately be at work with addictions to alcohol, nicotine, and perhaps some behavioral addictions. Although different substances affect different neural circuits, they all depend on the brain's remarkable capacity to learn from repeated experience.

The Future of Recovery

When I began studying addiction decades ago, much of our attention centered on withdrawal. Later, dopamine became the dominant framework. Increasingly, however, neuroadaptations provide a more comprehensive perspective.

Recovery is not simply a matter of the brain returning to where it was before cannabis. It is the brain establishing a new, healthier adaptive brain state without needing the drug that formerly defined the person's normal.

New treatments—including GLP-1 receptor agonists and perhaps psychedelic-assisted therapies for selected substance use disorders—may eventually help some patients achieve recovery more effectively. But medications alone cannot rebuild a life.

The same neuroplasticity that teaches dependence can also teach resilience. Given enough time, repeated healthy experience, and effective treatment, the adaptive brain can learn a new normal—not because it forgets what it previously learned, but because it gradually learns something better.

The most hopeful lesson from addiction neuroscience is that the same neuroplasticity that allows addiction to develop also allows recovery to occur.

Regular cannabis use teaches the brain one way of functioning. Recovery teaches it another.

Addiction is one expression of the brain's extraordinary capacity to learn from repeated experience. Recovery is another.

item.title: How to Raise a Child Other Kids Want to Be Friends With
item.description:
Friends

How to Raise a Child Other Kids Want to Be Friends With

The friendship skill parents often overlook.

Posted July 14, 2026

Key points
  • Friendships require compromise, adaptability, and tolerating disappointment.
  • Flexible people are often more likely to attract and maintain friendships.
  • Flexibility helps people recover when things do not go as planned.
Source: lisegagne/Getty Images Signature

Summer is here and there are some topics we revisit over and over again because they are basically ever-present, both for parents and their children. One such issue is friendship. It actually is an issue most of us deal with in our adult lives too—other people’s sensitivities and our own.

While summer is often a respite from many of the challenges that arise during the school year, it also creates opportunities for growth. Children typically have more unstructured interactions with siblings, friends, cousins, teammates, and peers. Those interactions create opportunities for parents to help children strengthen social skills in a more natural and organic way. For many of us, that is how learning happens most effectively—in the moment, rather than from a book or a lengthy lecture.

Previously, we looked at perspective taking and how friendship problems often arise when children make assumptions about another person’s thoughts, feelings, intentions, or motivations. Perspective taking encourages children to ask questions such as, “What might be going on for the other person?” or “What other explanation might there be for what happened?” It is fundamentally a skill of understanding. It helps children become more empathic, more considerate, and less likely to jump to conclusions. It can also reduce hurt feelings by reminding children that they do not always have enough information to know why something happened.

Flexibility addresses a different set of friendship challenges. Many social difficulties arise not because children misunderstand another person, but because things do not go the way they hoped. A friend wants to play something different. Plans change. They are not chosen first. They lose a game. They feel disappointed. In many of these situations, the issue is not understanding what happened. The issue is adapting to it.

Perspective taking helps children understand other people; flexibility helps children adjust when other people want something different than they do.

Over 15 years working with the Philadelphia Eagles, players would frequently talk about the qualities coaches valued most in players. While the list varied somewhat from coach to coach, coachability was always on the list.

Coachability is basically a willingness to accept feedback, direction, and suggestions without becoming defensive or resistant. It involves adapting when asked to do something differently, even when the change is not your first choice. It also reflects an understanding that what is best for the team is not always the same as what is best for the individual and that contributing to the success of the group may require a momentary personal sacrifice that is ultimately worth it.

Sustained friendships depend on many of the same qualities coaches value in athletes. Compromise is necessary. Plans change. Other people have preferences, priorities, and ideas of their own. Friends do not always want to do what we want to do. Sometimes maintaining a friendship requires us to adapt, accommodate someone else’s wishes, or put the relationship ahead of getting our own way. Without some degree of flexibility and the ability to tolerate the temporary disappointment that comes from not always getting our way, friendships are difficult to sustain.

Source: Kampus Productions/Pexels

Flexibility Makes Children Easier to Play With

One of the reasons flexibility is so important is that it makes children easier to play with.

Friendships involve a surprising amount of negotiation. Children decide what game to play, what rules to use, who goes first, what activity comes next, and how to resolve disagreements when they arise. Not surprisingly, children generally enjoy spending time with peers who can compromise, adapt, and occasionally go along with someone else’s idea.

This does not mean children should never express preferences or advocate for themselves. Rather, it means recognizing that successful friendships require some balance between our own wishes and the wishes of others.

Parents do not need to turn these moments into lengthy discussions. Often a brief question is enough:

  • “What would a good teammate do right now?”
  • “What would make someone want to play with you again?”
  • “Do you think someone is more or less likely to want to spend time with you if it is always what you want to do?”
  • “Do you think someone would want to hang out with you if you were always the one choosing the activity?”
  • “Can you imagine a compromise?”
  • “What’s Plan B?”
  • “Are you stuck on Plan A?”

Social coaching does not need to be lengthy. In fact, it is often more effective when it occurs in small doses. A brief observation. A question. A reminder. Often that is enough.

Source: vlader karpovich/pexels

Flexibility Helps Children Manage Disappointment

Flexibility does more than improve relationships. It also helps children manage the inevitable disappointments that occur in everyday life.

Children do not always win. They are not always chosen first. Their friends do not always want to do what they want to do. Plans change. Things do not always unfold as expected.

The less flexible a child is, the harder these situations often become. Sometimes children become so focused on not getting exactly what they want that they lose sight of what remains possible.

Recently, I asked a third grader whether he could tolerate a little less of what he wanted for 20 minutes in order to get most of what he wanted for the next 20.

Sometimes giving up a little gets us much more of what we want overall.

In many situations, flexibility is not about giving up what we want entirely. It is about accepting a temporary compromise that ultimately leaves everyone better off.

Parents can often help children think differently about these moments through simple questions:

  • “What would make this tolerable?”
  • “What would make this less disappointing?”
  • “Can you imagine a compromise?”
  • “Do you imagine everyone else always gets their way?”
  • “What do you think other children tell themselves when things don’t go their way?”
  • “Would it help if you told yourself, ‘I can do this for 15 minutes’?”
  • “Can you be disappointed and still move forward?”
  • “Which is more important right now: getting exactly what you want or preserving the relationship?”

The goal is not to eliminate disappointment. Disappointment is part of life. The goal is to help children tolerate it, recover from it, and adapt when circumstances do not unfold as they had hoped.

Source: fatcamera/Getty Images Signature

One of the advantages of summer is that it provides more opportunities to practice flexibility.

Family vacations, camps, sports, board games, playdates, sibling interactions, and everyday family decisions all create situations in which children may need to adjust when things do not go according to plan.

In fact, flexibility coaching may be most effective when it occurs in small doses. A brief observation. A question asked in passing. A reminder to consider another option.

Parents do not need to turn every situation into a lesson. Children generally do not need 20-minute lectures. Often they simply need help recognizing that disappointment is tolerable, compromise is possible, and getting slightly less of what they want in the moment may allow them to get much more of what they want over time.

Conclusion

Many friendship difficulties arise not because children lack social interest or good intentions, but because they struggle when things do not go their way. Flexibility helps children become easier to play with and better able to manage disappointment when situations unfold differently than expected.

Like perspective taking, flexibility is a skill that can be coached and strengthened over time. Summer provides countless opportunities to do so. Often all it takes is a brief question, a simple observation, or a reminder that friendships, like successful teams, depend on compromise, adaptability, and the ability to tolerate the temporary disappointment that sometimes accompanies not getting our way.

item.title: 8 Signs Someone Truly Feels Emotionally Safe With You
item.description:
Relationships

8 Signs Someone Truly Feels Emotionally Safe With You

The subtle behaviors that reveal trust, vulnerability, and genuine connection.

Posted July 14, 2026

Key points
  • Small, everyday interactions reveal whether someone truly feels safe enough to be themselves around you.
  • Feeling emotionally safe allows people to disagree, ask for support, and recover from conflict.
  • Secure bonds don't require constant entertainment, reassurance, or conversation.
Source: LightField Studios / Shutterstock

People don't wake up one morning and announce, "Congratulations, you've become my safe person."

The signs that a secure attachment is beginning to form are often subtle and develop gradually over time. A secure connection doesn't require grand gestures. It's built through hundreds of ordinary interactions that send the message: You can be your true self with me.

When people feel emotionally safe, they stop rehearsing every text message, apologizing for having feelings, pretending they're always fine, or worrying that one mistake will send you running.

Here are eight signs someone truly feels emotionally safe with you.

1. They Let You See Their Less Polished Side

At first, most people present the version of themselves they hope you'll like. Then, over time, they stop pretending they always wake up looking effortlessly attractive. They let you see them in mismatched pajamas, don't cancel on you just because they aren't feeling their best, and admit they're having a terrible week.

They confess they accidentally replied all to an email at work, cry during Pixar movies, or tell you about the embarrassing thing they did that still randomly pops into their head before they fall asleep.

They share their fears, insecurities, and mistakes without feeling the need to wrap everything in a joke or pretend everything is fine.

2. They Aren't Afraid to Disagree With You

People who fear rejection often avoid conflict. They are more likely to agree when they don't mean it or suppress their frustrations.

Someone who feels emotionally safe believes the relationship can survive disagreement. They trust that expressing a different opinion won't cost them your affection.

Ironically, healthy conflict often signals greater security than constant compliance and agreement.

Feeling safe doesn't mean always seeing eye to eye. It means trusting that one disagreement won't threaten the relationship. You stop worrying that every difficult conversation is going to end with someone walking away.

3. They Ask for Comfort Instead of Pretending They're Fine

Many people learned early in life that emotional needs were burdensome and therefore have a hard time asking for help.

As adults, asking for support can feel uncomfortable or even shameful.

When someone begins saying, "I've had a rough day," "Can I talk to you?" or "I just need a hug," they're showing a level of vulnerability that doesn't often come easily.

They're trusting that their emotional needs will be met with care rather than criticism, dismissal, or being told they're "too sensitive."

4. They Don't Feel the Need to Constantly Monitor Your Reactions

In emotionally unsafe relationships, people often become hypervigilant, constantly assessing the other person's emotional cues.

Couples analyze each other's tone, overthink text messages, replay conversations in their head, and wonder whether their partner suddenly became angry or lost interest because they replied with a period instead of an emoji.

As emotional safety grows, that constant scanning begins to ease. They become less preoccupied with reading between the lines because your words and actions are consistent.

5. They Tell You Things They Don't Tell Most People

Once people feel comfortable in relationships, they begin sharing childhood memories, painful experiences, family dynamics, regrets, dreams, and the stories they've sworn they'll "take to the grave."

When people trust that they won't be judged, dismissed, or have their experiences used against them later, opening up becomes much easier, and vulnerability no longer feels dangerous.

6. They Recover More Quickly After Conflict

Every relationship experiences misunderstandings and disagreements.

In secure connection, conflict becomes easier to navigate. Instead of assuming the relationship is ending, people become more willing to reconnect, apologize, listen, and work through the issue together.

Rather than viewing misunderstandings as permanent evidence that the relationship is doomed, they trust that most conflicts can be repaired. They no longer feel they have to earn your love by always saying the right thing or never disappointing you.

7. They Can Be Silent Together

Silence can feel painfully awkward when people don't feel safe with one another. Secure bonds don't require constant entertainment, reassurance, or conversation.

Reading together, driving in silence, sitting on opposite ends of the couch, or simply existing in the same room without feeling responsible for filling every quiet moment are all signs of comfort. No one feels obligated to ask, "So... what are you thinking about?" every 30 seconds.

8. They Start Becoming More Themselves

Rather than shrinking themselves to fit what they think you want, they slowly expand into who they already are.

They laugh more freely. They become more playful. They share more of their opinions, interests, quirks, and personality without wondering whether they're "too much."

In many ways, emotional safety is the foundation of every healthy relationship. It allows people to lower their defenses, speak honestly, recover from conflict, and gradually become more of themselves. After all, there are few greater gifts than creating a relationship where someone feels safe enough to be exactly who they are.

item.title: The Dangers of Purpose as a Proxy for Desire
item.description:
Emotions

The Dangers of Purpose as a Proxy for Desire

Your psychic vitality is essential for physical health.

Posted July 14, 2026

Key points
  • Purpose and desire are not the same, and the difference matters for health.
  • Psychic vitality may help protect the body from the effects of emotional suppression.
  • When emotions cannot be symbolized, the body may begin to express them.
  • Creativity, imagination, and emotional awareness help keep desire psychologically alive.

“In this world there are only two tragedies. One is not getting what one wants, and the other is getting it.”—Oscar Wilde

There is a darkness within desire that haunts most people. In its rawest form, desire is a wild creature whose constant yearning can unsettle both the individual and society. That is why we try to tame it, regulate it, or suppress it. Yet there is a hidden cost. When desire is stripped of imagination and emotional life rather than symbolically transformed, it may not only diminish our psychological vitality, but it may also leave the body more vulnerable to illness. Between unbridled expression and suppression lies a third path: symbolic elaboration, the psychological work that transforms desire into the psychic vitality that helps sustain both mind and body.

Source: Credit:LiudmylaSupynska/iStockphoto

The Seduction of Purpose

The evidence for purpose is seductive — and real. In Japan, researchers studying ikigai — roughly, "that which makes life worth living" — found that adults without it had a 50 percent higher risk of dying over seven years.1 A 2026 meta-analysis of nearly half a million participants confirmed the global pattern: Purpose in life was associated with an approximately 30 percent lower mortality risk, even after controlling for behavioral and clinical risk factors.2 Purpose, it seems, keeps us alive. What could possibly be dangerous about it?

Purpose, as Aristotle understood it, was never a goal you set. It was the inner movement of a living thing toward its fullest expression — the telos, an intrinsic drive woven into the organism itself. 3 But the modern science of purpose has replaced this with something thinner: conscious intention, goal-directedness, a reason to get out of bed. The scales that produced those impressive mortality statistics do not measure Aristotelian flourishing. They measure whether you can articulate a plan.4 And a plan, however earnest, is not the same as the deeper psychic vitality that keeps the body alive.

The problem is that purpose and psychic vitality are not the same thing. Clinicians working in psychosomatic medicine noticed this decades ago. Pierre Marty and the Paris Psychosomatic School described patients who were goal-directed, productive, even high-functioning — yet their bodies were at risk. He called their cognitive style pensée opératoire: mechanical, fact-bound thinking stripped of fantasy, imagination, and emotional elaboration.5 It is like a mind running on purpose with only a destination in mind. According to the Paris School, when emotional experience can no longer be processed psychologically, the risk of serious physical illness increases.5

The closely related construct of alexithymia — difficulty identifying emotions, constricted imagination, externally oriented thinking — has been consistently linked to somatization, chronic pain, and medically unexplained symptoms.6 Somatization can thus be understood as the body's expression of what the mind cannot elaborate symbolically — unsymbolized emotional arousal that finds no outlet in fantasy, language, or relational life.8 A person can have every reason to live and still lack the psychic vitality to do so. What is missing is not purpose. What is missing is desire.

Desire and Its Symbolic Life

If purpose without psychic depth leaves the body vulnerable, what protects it? Marty believed it was the mind's capacity for symbolic imagination—the ability to transform raw emotional energy into dreams, images, and meaning rather than allowing it to be expressed through the body.9 Rosenberg called this process a "guardian of life," arguing that when it fails, the body becomes increasingly vulnerable.10

Clinical evidence supports this view. Improving mentalization—the ability to understand one's own and others' mental states—reduces depression, anxiety, and physical symptoms during psychosomatic rehabilitation.12 Short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy, which restores symbolic and emotional processing, significantly reduces physical symptoms, with benefits lasting over time.13 Even expressive writing—putting emotions into words—reduces physical symptoms. In one study of 277 kidney cancer patients, it improved physical functioning and reduced symptoms at 10 months.14

The processes that protect the body are surprisingly ordinary. One is daydreaming, which occupies 30 to 50 percent of waking life and, when focused on close relationships, increases happiness, love, and connection.15 They include creativity, intimacy, and naming emotions—the symbolic life of desire that allows the mind, rather than the body, to carry emotional experience.

Wilde's paradox — that getting what you want is as tragic as not getting it — is not cynicism. It is a precise description of desire's nature: desire is never finally satisfied, and that is its power. The tragedy is not in wanting. It is in believing that fulfillment will end the wanting, or worse, in ceasing to want at all. What Aristotle called purpose was never a destination — it was the living movement toward fullness. Modern science kept the word but lost the movement. That movement is desire. The prescription is not to abandon your goals but to tend the inner life that sustains them — to daydream, to feel, to let the imagination do its quiet, vital work. Your body is listening.
